This schedule credits interest heavily toward the start of the loan, so paying off early refunds less unearned interest than the actuarial method. On a $15,000 loan at 7% APR over 48 months paid off after 12 payments, the lender keeps $28.65 more in interest under the Rule of 78. Federal law under 15 U.S.C. 1615 requires a refund at least as favorable as the actuarial method only for precomputed consumer credit transactions longer than 61 months that were made after September 30, 1993. In our internal modeling, we compared the Rule of 78 with the actuarial method on the same loans to see what an early payoff costs. For a $15,000 loan at 7% over 48 months, paying the balance in full after 12 payments yields an unearned interest refund of $1,269.31 under the Rule of 78 compared with $1,297.96 under the actuarial method. That difference leaves $28.65 more with the lender. Enter your own loan in the calculator below, or read the month-by-month table further down, to check these figures. Share Interactive — edit any field How the Rule of 78 Splits Your Interest A precomputed loan calculates the total finance charge at origination and adds it to the principal before spreading the total across equal monthly installments. The standard monthly installment is calculated using the principal, monthly rate, and number of payments. You can inspect equal monthly installments and standard amortization schedules with our loan payment calculator . The total finance charge equals the monthly payment multiplied by the number of months minus the principal amount borrowed. When you prepay a precomputed loan, the lender calculates how much of that total finance charge has been earned and how much must be refunded. The Rule of 78 weights each payment's interest using the sum of the digits of the loan term. For a loan of n months, the denominator S equals n(n + 1) / 2. On a 12-month loan, S equals 12 + 11 + ... + 1, which totals 78. That calculation gives the rule its name. On a 48-month loan, S equals 1,176. In month j, the lender earns a fraction of the finance charge equal to (n - j + 1) / S. After k payments, the earned interest fraction is k(2n - k + 1) / (n(n + 1)). The refund of unearned interest is the total finance charge minus this earned interest amount. Consider our baseline example of a $15,000 loan at 7% APR over 48 months with a total finance charge of $2,241.30. In month 1, the Rule of 78 assigns 48 / 1,176 of the total interest, which equals $91.48. Month 48 is credited just $1.91. Under the actuarial method, month 1 interest is $87.50, based on the initial balance multiplied by the monthly rate, while month 48 interest is $2.08. After 12 payments, the Rule of 78 has earned $971.99, or 43.37% of the finance charge, while the actuarial method has earned $943.34, or 42.09%. The actuarial method applies each payment first to accumulated interest on the actual remaining balance and then subtracts the remainder from the unpaid principal. The calculator assumes a fixed-rate precomputed loan, level monthly payments, payoff immediately after a scheduled payment, and no additional fees. It does not account for specific contract terms, state-level regulations, or rebate-on-default rules. For terms exceeding 61 months, the calculator displays a notice stating that the result is a formula illustration because federal law restricts this practice on consumer loans. What Early Payoff Costs Under the Rule of 78 The month-by-month table illustrates the first 12 months of interest credited on a $15,000 loan at 7% APR over 48 months, while the calculator lists every month across the full schedule. Month Rule of 78 interest Actuarial interest 1 $91.48 $87.50 2 $89.58 $85.92 3 $87.67 $84.32 4 $85.76 $82.72 5 $83.86 $81.10 6 $81.95 $79.48 7 $80.05 $77.85 8 $78.14 $76.21 9 $76.23 $74.56 10 $74.33 $72.90 11 $72.42 $71.23 12 $70.52 $69.55 Loan Total finance charge Paid off after payment Extra interest kept $5,000 at 6% over 24 months $318.47 12 $1.64 $15,000 at 3% over 48 months $936.72 12 $5.23 $15,000 at 7% over 48 months $2,241.30 12 $28.65 $15,000 at 7% over 48 months $2,241.30 24 $26.26 $15,000 at 7% over 48 months $2,241.30 42 $3.30 $15,000 at 7% over 48 months $2,241.30 48 $0.00 $25,000 at 8% over 60 months $5,414.59 12 $88.13 The dollar gap between the two methods is widest during the earlier and middle months of repayment. On the $15,000 loan at 7% over 48 months, the lender keeps $28.65 more after 12 payments and $26.26 more after 24 payments. By payment 42, that extra interest drops to $3.30. By payment 48, both methods have credited the entire finance charge, reducing the difference to $0.00. Larger loans, higher interest rates, and longer maturities widen the gap in unearned interest. On a $25,000 loan at 8% over 60 months, paying off after 12 payments leaves $88.13 more with the lender under the Rule of 78. Conversely, small loans or lower rates produce small differences. A $5,000 loan at 6% over 24 months paid off at month 12 results in a $1.64 difference, while a $15,000 loan at 3% over 48 months paid off at month 12 costs $5.23 more. As a pure formula illustration, a $30,000 loan at 9% over 72 months paid off after 24 payments would produce a $227.82 difference, but federal law restricts precomputed terms of that length for consumer loans. Is the Rule of 78 Legal? Federal law under 15 U.S.C. 1615(b) requires that any refund of interest on a precomputed consumer credit transaction with a term exceeding 61 months consummated after September 30, 1993, must be computed using a method at least as favorable as the actuarial method. This requirement means the Rule of 78 cannot be used to reduce an early payoff refund below the actuarial level on those long-term consumer loans. It is not a blanket ban across all credit transactions. Under 15 U.S.C. 1615(a)(1), if a consumer prepays the financed amount in full under any consumer credit transaction, the creditor must promptly refund any unearned portion of the interest charge. This rule applies regardless of whether prepayment occurs through refinancing, consolidation, restructuring, or creditor acceleration. Under 1615(a)(2), no refund is required if the total refund amount is less than $1. Federal statute 15 U.S.C. 1615(b) does not address terms of 61 months or less, leaving those shorter loans subject to state laws and individual contract provisions. We take no position on state laws governing credit terms. Under 15 U.S.C. 1615(c), a creditor must provide a payoff statement within 5 days of a consumer request detailing the amount needed to prepay in full, including any required refund. A consumer is entitled to one free payoff statement per year. Who This Is Not For This calculation does not apply to simple-interest loans. According to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) , simple interest is far more common for auto loans than precomputed interest. On a simple-interest loan, interest accrues daily or monthly on the actual outstanding balance. Borrowers looking to calculate extra payment savings on a simple-interest auto loan should use our auto loan early payoff calculator instead. This calculator also does not cover business credit or loans originated outside the United States. Subsection (b) of 15 U.S.C. 1615 covers precomputed consumer credit transactions, and business loans follow rules this page does not cover. Borrowers who need a formal legal interpretation of an existing financing agreement cannot rely solely on a mathematical model. For a term of 61 months or less, the contract and state law decide. A written payoff statement from the lender shows the refund it will actually give, and 15 U.S.C. 1615(c) entitles you to one free statement each year. What Would Change Our Answer A loan contract based on simple interest or the actuarial method will invalidate this comparison. If an agreement does not use precomputed interest, interest is calculated solely on the outstanding principal balance rather than front-loaded via sum-of-the-digits arithmetic. In that case, interest is charged on the actual outstanding balance, so the Rule of 78 split does not apply. A precomputed consumer loan with a term exceeding 61 months also alters the outcome under federal statute. Loans exceeding 61 months consummated after September 30, 1993, must provide a refund at least as favorable as the actuarial method under 15 U.S.C. 1615(b). Any lender gain shown on such a loan is only a formula illustration. Specific state laws or contract terms can also dictate different rebate requirements. Finally, an official payoff statement from the lender showing a different calculated figure supersedes any estimate from this model. Our Takeaway Based on our internal modeling, the Rule of 78 accelerates interest charges into the early months of a precomputed loan, reducing the refund of unearned interest when you pay the balance off early. That cost difference ranges from a few dollars on small, short-term loans ($1.64 on a 24-month loan at 6%) to dozens of dollars on larger balances ($28.65 on our 48-month baseline and $88.13 on a 60-month loan at 8%), eventually tapering to $0.00 at the end of the term. Federal law requires an actuarial-or-better refund only for precomputed consumer loans longer than 61 months made after September 30, 1993. To see how your own financing is affected, run your loan terms through the rule of 78 calculator and compare the result against your lender's written payoff statement. Frequently asked questions What is the Rule of 78? The Rule of 78 is a method used on precomputed loans to allocate interest charges across payment periods. It assigns larger shares of interest to early payments based on the sum of the digits of the loan term. This means paying off early refunds less unearned interest than the actuarial method. What is the Rule of 78 formula? The formula credits each month with a share of the finance charge equal to the number of months from that month to the end of the loan, divided by the sum of all the month numbers in the term. For an n-month loan, the sum is S = n(n + 1) / 2. Each month j is allocated a fraction of the total finance charge equal to (n - j + 1) / S. Can you show a Rule of 78 example? On a $15,000 loan at 7% over 48 months, the total finance charge is $2,241.30. In month 1, the Rule of 78 credits $91.48 of interest, compared with $87.50 under the actuarial method. After 12 payments, paying off the loan yields a $1,269.31 refund under the Rule of 78, leaving the lender with $28.65 more. Is the Rule of 78 legal? Federal law under 15 U.S.C. 1615(b) requires an actuarial-or-better refund on precomputed consumer credit transactions longer than 61 months consummated after September 30, 1993. The statute does not address terms of 61 months or less. Individual state laws and credit contracts determine whether it can be used for shorter loans. Does the Rule of 78 apply to car loans? It applies only if the auto financing agreement is written as a precomputed interest loan. The CFPB notes that precomputed interest is uncommon on auto loans, while simple interest is far more standard. Simple-interest auto loans calculate interest on the unpaid daily balance rather than using the Rule of 78. How do I find out what my lender will refund if I pay off early? You can request an official payoff statement directly from your loan servicer. Under 15 U.S.C. 1615(c), creditors must provide a statement showing the payoff balance and any unearned interest refund within 5 days of your request. Consumers are entitled to receive one such statement each year without charge. How is the Rule of 78 different from simple interest? Simple-interest loans charge interest strictly based on the outstanding principal balance as payments are made. Precomputed loans calculate the total finance charge upfront and allocate it across payments using a set formula. With the Rule of 78, more of each early payment goes toward interest, reducing your savings if you prepay. Why does the Rule of 78 refund less when I pay off early? The Rule of 78 front-loads interest by crediting larger portions of the total finance charge to earlier months. By the time you pay off the balance, the lender has already recognized more earned interest than under standard amortization. This leaves a smaller remaining unearned interest balance to refund. Enter your balance, APR, term, and monthly extra amount in the calculator above. It instantly shows your new payoff date and total interest savings, helping you decide whether paying off your car loan early is worth it for you. $552 monthly payment $1,332 total interest $529 saved with extra payments Share Interactive — edit any field How it's calculated The calculator estimates your savings by applying your extra payment straight to the loan principal each month. A smaller principal means less interest accrues, so the loan ends sooner. It compares your original schedule against the faster one and reports the gap in dollars and months. Because most of each early payment goes to interest, attacking the principal early has the biggest effect. A worked example Say you owe $18,000 at 6.5% APR with 36 months left. Your scheduled payment is $551.68 a month. Add $200 extra and your first month puts $654.18 toward principal and just $97.50 toward interest. Keep it up and you pay the loan off in 26 months, about 2 years and 2 months. Total interest drops to $1,332. That saves you $529 in interest and 10 months of payments. Common mistakes to avoid Draining your emergency fund to pay the loan off early. Experian lists this as a reason to wait, since you may need cash for surprises. Paying off a low-rate car loan while carrying high-rate credit card debt. Pay the highest-rate balance first, where average card APRs far exceed auto rates. Skipping the prepayment penalty check. The CFPB notes some contracts charge a fee for early payoff, which can erase your savings. Assuming extra cash always lowers the principal. Tell your lender to apply extra money to principal, not toward your next scheduled payment. Ignoring a precomputed-interest loan. With these, interest is set upfront, so early payoff may save less than a simple-interest loan, and the Rule of 78 calculator shows the refund difference. Frequently asked questions Is using a pay off car loan early calculator worth it? Yes. It shows your exact interest and time savings before you commit extra cash. In our example, $200 extra each month saves $529 in interest and clears the loan 10 months sooner. Seeing real numbers helps you weigh early payoff against other goals. Does paying off a car loan early hurt your credit? It may cause a small, temporary dip. Experian says paying off a car loan early can drop your score for a few months because it reduces your open accounts and credit mix. The dip usually fades, and reducing debt helps you long term. Should I pay off my car loan early or invest instead? Compare your loan APR to what a safe investment earns. If your car loan rate is higher than a guaranteed return like a high-yield savings account, paying it off often wins. If the rate is very low, investing may grow your money faster. Will I be charged a fee for paying my car loan off early? Sometimes. The CFPB says some auto loan contracts include a prepayment penalty to discourage early payoff. Check your loan agreement or ask your lender before making large extra payments, since a fee can reduce your savings. Where should I make extra payments go on my loan? Direct extra money to your principal. The CFPB explains that paying down principal faster lowers the interest you owe. Tell your lender or servicer to apply the extra amount to principal, not toward your next scheduled payment. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. mainEntity.name: Is using a pay off car loan early calculator worth it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. It shows your exact interest and time savings before you commit extra cash. In our example, $200 extra each month saves $529 in interest and clears the loan 10 months sooner. Seeing real numbers helps you weigh early payoff against other goals.

mainEntity.name: Does paying off a car loan early hurt your credit?

acceptedAnswer.text: It may cause a small, temporary dip. Experian says paying off a car loan early can drop your score for a few months because it reduces your open accounts and credit mix. The dip usually fades, and reducing debt helps you long term.

mainEntity.name: Should I pay off my car loan early or invest instead?

acceptedAnswer.text: Compare your loan APR to what a safe investment earns. If your car loan rate is higher than a guaranteed return like a high-yield savings account, paying it off often wins. If the rate is very low, investing may grow your money faster.

mainEntity.name: Will I be charged a fee for paying my car loan off early?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sometimes. The CFPB says some auto loan contracts include a prepayment penalty to discourage early payoff. Check your loan agreement or ask your lender before making large extra payments, since a fee can reduce your savings.

mainEntity.name: Where should I make extra payments go on my loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Direct extra money to your principal. The CFPB explains that paying down principal faster lowers the interest you owe. Tell your lender or servicer to apply the extra amount to principal, not toward your next scheduled payment.

Enter your remaining balance, rate, and term above, then add an extra monthly amount or switch to choosing a payoff date. The calculator will show your new timeline next to the original one. Extra payments work because a personal loan charges interest only on what you still owe. Every extra dollar you put toward principal now stops earning the lender interest in every month that follows. Share Interactive — edit any field How it's calculated The calculator above takes your remaining balance, interest rate, and remaining term to find your scheduled monthly payment, the same fully amortizing math your lender uses. From there it runs two payoff schedules side by side: one at your normal payment, and one with your extra amount added straight to principal every month, then shows the gap between them in dollars and months. Switch to "I want a payoff date" mode, and the calculator works backward instead. Pick how many months you want left on the loan, and it solves for the exact extra payment that gets you there, using the same amortization formula in reverse. Either direction, the underlying math never changes. Every dollar that goes to principal early stops accruing interest for every remaining month of the loan, which is why even a modest extra payment can meaningfully shorten a multi-year loan. A worked example Say you have $15,000 left on a personal loan at 12.5% APR with 48 months remaining. Your scheduled payment is about $398.70 a month, and paying only that amount takes about 49 months and costs roughly $4,138 in interest before the loan is gone, the extra month coming from how a fixed payment amortizes a balance that started with a small rounding gap. Add $100 a month in extra payments, and the same loan clears in about 37 months instead, saving roughly $1,048 in interest over the life of the loan. Switch to payoff-date mode and ask for that same loan to be gone in 30 months instead, and the calculator solves for the extra payment directly: about $186 a month on top of the scheduled payment, cutting total interest to roughly $2,543, rather than making you guess and check different extra amounts by hand. Common mistakes to avoid Assuming every lender applies an extra payment to principal automatically. Some apply it toward next month's payment instead unless you specifically mark it for principal, so confirm your lender's process before sending extra money. Not confirming a prepayment penalty first. Most personal loan lenders don't charge one, but the CFPB confirms a few loan contracts still include one, so check your agreement before committing to a payoff plan. Comparing only the interest saved, without weighing it against other financial priorities. An extra loan payment competes with an emergency fund, a 401(k) match, or a higher-interest credit card balance, so pay down the highest-rate debt first if you're carrying more than one. Ignoring the loan's origination fee when judging the real cost of the loan itself. The fee already came out of your original disbursement, not your remaining balance, so it doesn't change the payoff math above, but it does change what the loan actually cost you; our personal loan calculator accounts for that fee separately. Picking a token extra amount instead of running the actual numbers. Twenty extra dollars a month barely moves the timeline on a large balance, while the same amount makes a real dent on a small one, so run your specific balance and rate instead of guessing at a round number. Frequently asked questions How much do extra payments actually save on a personal loan? It depends on your balance, rate, and how much extra you add, but the effect compounds fast. On a $15,000 loan at 12.5% APR with 48 months left, a $100 monthly extra payment saves roughly $1,048 in interest and clears the loan about a year sooner. Enter your own numbers in the calculator above to see your exact savings. Do personal loans have prepayment penalties? Most don't, but some still do. The CFPB confirms a prepayment penalty is legal on some loan contracts, so check your loan agreement or ask your lender directly before committing to an extra-payment plan, rather than assuming your loan works like most others. If the loan is precomputed, how the Rule of 78 works decides how much interest an early payoff refunds. Does my lender automatically apply extra money to principal? Not always. Some lenders apply an extra payment toward your next month's bill instead of your principal balance unless you specifically designate it for principal, often through an option on the payment screen or a note with a mailed payment. Confirm the process with your lender before sending extra money, since a payment applied the wrong way won't shorten your payoff the way you expect. Should I pay extra on a personal loan or invest the money instead? Compare your loan's interest rate to what you'd realistically earn investing instead. A personal loan charging 12% or more is a rate few investments reliably beat after taxes, so extra payments usually win at that range. At a lower personal loan rate, say under 7%, investing a long-term retirement contribution can be the better math, especially if it captures an employer 401(k) match first. How is this different from the regular personal loan calculator? This calculator solves a payoff question for a loan you already have: how much an extra payment saves, or what extra payment hits a target payoff date. Our personal loan calculator answers a different question, what a new loan actually costs once its origination fee is factored into the real, effective APR. Use this one once you're already repaying a loan and want to speed that up. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions.
